rules.t: A candidate must win a majority of the votes cast. If no one does, the top two meet in a runoff on the 28th day after the election. Only presidential electors are exempt.

links.title: O.C.G.A. § 21-2-501, majority and runoffs (Justia)

rules.t: A candidate trailing by no more than 0.5% of the votes cast for the office can request a recount in writing within two business days after certification. Requests for statewide or multi-county races go to the Secretary of State, who orders a recount in every county; single-county races go to the county. For ballot questions, the Constitutional Amendments Publication Board may call one.

links.title: O.C.G.A. § 21-2-495, recounts (Justia)

rules.t: A 2026 law (SB 3EX, signed June 25) requires a hand recount of every ballot in every county, with no request needed, when the race for Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, Attorney General, School Superintendent, or Insurance, Agriculture or Labor Commissioner appears first or second on the ballot and is decided by 0.5% or less. On the Nov. 3 ballot U.S. Senate is first and Governor second, so only the Governor's race qualifies. The Secretary of State must order the recount within two business days after the Nov. 9 county certification deadline; the state repays counties that finish within 17 days.

links.title: O.C.G.A. § 21-2-495, recounts, as amended by SB 3EX (Justia, 2025 Code of Georgia)
SB 3EX as signed (Office of the Governor)

rules.t: Before certification, counties run risk-limiting audits, hand-checking random samples of paper ballots to confirm the machine count (risk limit of no more than 6% in 2026). The audited races are the top race on the ballot (U.S. Senate this year), U.S. House, Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State and Attorney General, plus one more statewide race chosen by majority vote of the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, House Speaker and the two minority leaders, or by the State Election Board chair if they don't agree by 11 a.m. on the Thursday after the election.

rules.t: A bill needs a majority of all members of each chamber, not just of those voting: 29 of 56 senators and 91 of 180 representatives. Overriding a governor's veto takes two-thirds of all members: 38 senators and 120 representatives.

rules.t: The House elects its Speaker from among its members. The Lieutenant Governor presides over the Senate as its president, and senators elect a President Pro Tempore. The Senate writes its own rules: its majority took committee-appointment powers from Democratic Lt. Gov. Mark Taylor in 2003 and from Republican Lt. Gov. Casey Cagle after the 2010 election.

rules.t: When a legislative seat becomes vacant during a session, or between 60 days before the first-year November election and the second-year session, the Governor issues a writ within 10 days for a special election 30 to 60 days later. After the first-year session ends, the Governor may call one at any time for a date at least 30 days out and no later than 60 days before that November; after the second-year session, calling one is at the Governor's discretion. During a special session, the writ is due within two days of the call, or within five days of a later vacancy.

rules.t: An amendment passes with a majority of those voting on it and takes effect on the January 1 after it passes, unless it says otherwise.

caveats: georgia.gov tells voters to fix a provisional-ballot problem "by the end of the next day"; the statute gives counties until three days after the election (Nov 6) to decide those ballots. Voters should check with their county.
Recount and contest deadlines run from certification, so their exact dates depend on when results are certified.
The 2003 and 2010 Senate precedents come from news accounts, not statute text.
Election-law text was checked on Nov. 4-5, 2026 against the current Code and the General Assembly's enacted acts, including the June 2026 special session.
